title: Circumcision, Passover, and the Commander of the LORD's Army
summary: As the kings of Canaan lose heart, the LORD tells Joshua to circumcise the generation born in the wilderness, and he does so at Gilgal. God declares that he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt. Israel keeps the Passover on the plains of Jericho, eats the produce of the land, and the manna stops. Near Jericho Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who identifies himself as commander of the LORD's army and tells Joshua to remove his sandals, for the ground is holy.
story: Israel has crossed the Jordan and set up memorial stones at Gilgal. Before any battle is fought, the people must be restored to their covenant identity. The generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised, and they had not, as far as the text tells us, kept the Passover since the second year after the exodus (Numbers 9). Now both covenant signs are renewed on the soil of the promised land. The wilderness provision of manna ends, and Israel begins to eat from the land itself. The chapter closes with Joshua's encounter with the heavenly commander, which prepares for chapter 6: the battle for Jericho will be the LORD's battle, fought on his terms.
historical:
The chapter is set at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho in early spring, just days after the crossing on the tenth of the first month (4:19). Passover fell on the fourteenth day of that month (verse 10), as Exodus 12:6 prescribed. Unleavened bread and roasted grain (verse 11) would have come from the spring barley harvest, the first crop of the year in the Jordan valley. Exodus 16:35 had already said that Israel ate manna for forty years until they came to the border of Canaan, and Joshua 5:12 records the moment it ended.

The explanation in verses 4 to 7 recalls Numbers 14, where God swore that the adult generation who refused to enter the land would die in the wilderness. Circumcision had apparently lapsed during the wilderness years; the text does not say why, and interpreters have suggested the hardships of travel or the broken status of the rebellious generation. The name Gibeath-haaraloth (verse 3) means the hill of foreskins, a blunt place name marking what happened there.
cultural:
Circumcision was practiced by several peoples of the ancient Near East, including Egyptians, but Israel gave it a distinct meaning as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:9-14). Flint knives (verse 2) were used for circumcision long after metal tools were common, perhaps because of the rite's antiquity or because flint was ritually preferred; Zipporah also used a flint in Exodus 4:25. Performing circumcision on adult men just before a military campaign left them vulnerable for several days (verse 8; compare Genesis 34:25), which makes the act one of trust in God's protection.

The reproach of Egypt (verse 9) has been read in several ways: the shame of slavery, the taunts Egyptians might make if Israel perished in the wilderness (Exodus 32:12, Numbers 14:13-16), or the disgrace of the uncircumcised, disobedient generation. The place name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew verb galal, to roll, and the text connects them. Removing sandals in a holy place (verse 15) was a sign of reverence and humility, and the command repeats almost word for word what God said to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5). Later Jewish tradition held that the priests also served barefoot in the sanctuary.
literary: The chapter has four short scenes framed by fear and holiness. It opens with the Canaanite kings' hearts melting (verse 1), echoing Rahab's words, and it closes with Joshua falling on his face before the commander (verse 14). In between, three transitions mark the change from wilderness to land: circumcision renews the covenant sign, Passover renews the covenant memory, and the end of manna marks a new way of being fed. The final scene is abrupt and mysterious. Joshua asks a straightforward military question, whose side are you on, and receives a surprising answer: “Neither.” The commander has come not to join Israel's side but to lead the LORD's army, and Joshua's proper posture is worship. The echo of Moses at the burning bush confirms again that God is with Joshua as he was with Moses.

outline.t: The kings of Canaan lose heart
Circumcision at Gilgal and the reproach rolled away
Passover and the end of the manna
The commander of the LORD's army

doctrines.note: Before taking the land, Israel receives again the signs of the covenant: circumcision and Passover. Their identity as God's people comes before their mission.

Circumcision and Passover were the Old Testament's covenant signs and meals, marking entry into God's people and remembrance of his rescue. Christians have long connected them with baptism and the Lord's Supper, though traditions differ on how closely the signs correspond.
The commander tells Joshua that the place is holy. Before Israel fights, its leader must worship, and the war to come is the LORD's, not Joshua's.
Manna stops the day after Israel eats the produce of the land. God's provision changes form but does not end, moving from miraculous bread to the ordinary harvest.

words.note: Galal, to roll. God says he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, and the place is named Gilgal, which sounds like this verb (verse 9). Place names in the Old Testament often carry such wordplay, tying a location to a memory.
Cherpah, reproach, disgrace, or taunt. It refers to shame that others can point to. Whatever exactly the reproach of Egypt was, God removes it as Israel is restored to its covenant sign in the land.

Sar, a ruler, prince, or commander. The figure is the commander of the LORD's army (verses 14-15). In Daniel the same word is used for heavenly princes, including Michael. The army of the LORD in view is probably the heavenly host.
Qodesh, holiness or a holy thing. The place is holy because of who is present. The same idea governed the burning bush, where God first revealed his name to Moses.

christ: Paul writes that true circumcision is “a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code” (Romans 2:29), and Colossians 2:11-12 describes believers as circumcised with a circumcision not done by human hands, buried with Christ in baptism. The renewal at Gilgal, where a generation receives the covenant sign before entering the inheritance, becomes in the New Testament a picture of the inner renewal Christ brings. Passover, kept here in the land for the first time, points forward to the meal Jesus shared with his disciples at Passover on the night he was betrayed, and Paul calls Christ “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jesus also speaks of himself as the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna (John 6:32-35). The identity of the commander of the LORD's army is debated: many early Christian writers saw him as the Son of God before his incarnation, while others see a high angel. The text itself leaves him mysterious.

hard.q: Who is the commander of the LORD's army, and why does he accept Joshua's worship?
hard.a: The text does not name him, and interpreters have offered several views. Many church fathers and later Christian interpreters identified him as a Christophany, an appearance of the Son of God before the incarnation, pointing out that he accepts Joshua's reverence and declares the ground holy, as God did at the burning bush. Others identify him as the angel of the LORD, a figure who in several passages speaks as God himself (Genesis 16, Exodus 3), leaving open how that figure relates to God. Still others see a created angel, perhaps Michael, whom Daniel calls a great prince; on this view Joshua's bowing is a gesture of respect, and the holiness of the ground comes from God's presence rather than from the messenger. The encounter breaks off without a battle plan, and 6:2 continues with the LORD speaking directly, which some take as a sign that the commander and the LORD are closely identified. The main point is not in dispute: the LORD's army is not on Israel's side; Israel must be on the LORD's.

questions: Before a single battle, Israel is called to renew the signs of the covenant. What practices remind you of who you belong to before you take on a challenge?
The manna stopped once Israel could eat from the land. How has God's provision in your life changed form over time?
Joshua asks whether the commander is for Israel or its enemies and hears 'neither.' What changes when we ask whether we are on God's side instead of whether God is on ours?
